title: Microsoft Unveils MAI-DxO Diagnostic Orchestrator in Science
description: Microsoft unveiled MAI-DxO, a GPT-5-powered Diagnostic Orchestrator that outdiagnosed doctors in simulated clinical tests published in Science.
dek: Published in Science, Microsoft's multi-agent system topped generalist doctors in diagnostic accuracy and is heading to hospital trials in Boston.
keyTakeaways: Microsoft published findings in Science showing its multi-agent Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO) diagnosed complex NEJM cases with 83.2% accuracy, compared to 36.1% for generalist physicians using references.
The system operates sequentially, asking questions, ordering tests, and debating hypotheses across multiple AI agents to simulate a clinical panel.
Microsoft plans to launch clinical evaluations with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston within the next couple of months.

Researchers noted key limitations: the tests were simulated on past records, compared only against generalists rather than specialist teams, and real-world clinical deployment will require rigorous validation.
body:
Microsoft researchers have developed an artificial intelligence diagnostic framework that substantially outperformed practicing generalist physicians in simulated diagnostic evaluations. The findings, published on October 22, 2026, in the peer-reviewed journal [Science](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/1016690/suleyman-microsoft-diagnostic-orchestrator-science-medical-superintelligence), evaluated the Microsoft AI Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO). The system uses multiple agents powered by OpenAI's GPT-5 to step through patient cases, gather evidence, order medical tests, and deliberate toward a final diagnosis.

The publication marks an early milestone in Microsoft AI's broader initiative to pursue what leadership terms medical superintelligence—systems capable of surpassing the reasoning and care coordination of contemporary human-led medical networks. The paper, titled "Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models," follows an earlier non-peer-reviewed preprint released on arXiv the previous year, as reported by [Gizmodo](https://gizmodo.com/microsoft-says-its-new-ai-is-more-than-twice-as-good-at-diagnosing-diseases-as-doctors-2000829562).

## How the Diagnostic Orchestrator Mimics Clinical Panels

Traditional artificial intelligence benchmarks in medicine typically provide a model with an entire clinical history, laboratory panel, and imaging summary all at once. In contrast, real clinical practice requires sequential reasoning. A clinician begins with a chief complaint, asks targeted questions, selectively orders diagnostic tests, and revises potential diagnoses while weighing risks and costs.

[[FIG1]]

To replicate this clinical reality, Microsoft introduced the Sequential Diagnosis Benchmark, or SDBench, which the company plans to open-source. Within this benchmark, the Diagnostic Orchestrator assigns specific responsibilities to distinct agents. As detailed by [The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/1016690/suleyman-microsoft-diagnostic-orchestrator-science-medical-superintelligence), individual agents propose candidate diagnoses, select cost-effective lab tests, challenge baseline assumptions, and debate findings. Researchers noted that this cooperative structure helps mitigate human cognitive errors, such as premature closure or anchoring on an initial hypothesis.

## Diagnostic Accuracy on NEJM and Emergency Department Cases

Microsoft tested MAI-DxO across two clinical datasets: challenging case records published in The New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) and real-world emergency department admissions from the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, drawn from the MIMIC-IV-ED database.

On the NEJM cases, which represent rare or diagnostically elusive conditions, MAI-DxO attained an accuracy of 83 percent, according to [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/22/microsofts-mustafa-suleyman-says-its-ai-outperforms-doctors-on-hard-cases-as-he-chases-medical-superintelligence/). In comparison, practicing generalist physicians who had access to reference textbooks and online search tools scored 36.1 percent. When generalist physicians were evaluated without reference materials, their accuracy dropped to approximately 22 percent, meaning MAI-DxO was nearly four times as accurate in that specific setting.

In emergency department cases, MAI-DxO scored 80.3 percent accuracy, whereas human generalist physicians achieved an average of 46.8 percent—making the orchestrator 1.7 times more accurate on those records, according to a blog post by [Microsoft AI](https://microsoft.ai/news/building-medical-superintelligence/). Microsoft also reported that the system achieved these results while requesting fewer simulated tests and procedures, cutting estimated case costs by one-half to one-third.

## Model Scaling, Costs, and the Role of GPT-5

The study revealed that while underlying foundation models drive substantial reasoning capability, multi-agent orchestration provides critical optimization. Microsoft tested MAI-DxO against models from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and DeepSeek, with top performance delivered by OpenAI's GPT-5 and GPT-5.5, according to [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/22/microsofts-mustafa-suleyman-says-its-ai-outperforms-doctors-on-hard-cases-as-he-chases-medical-superintelligence/).

[[FIG2]]

When evaluated on complex cases using a simple prompt, standalone GPT-5 scored 78.9 percent accuracy at an estimated computational cost of approximately $8,400 per case. Adding the DxO orchestration layer increased accuracy to 83 percent while reducing computational expense by roughly $3,000. For GPT-5.5, a model released in April 2026, DxO raised accuracy from 72 percent to nearly 87 percent on complex cases.

The orchestration boost was most pronounced on smaller models. Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash jumped from 46.4 percent on its own to nearly 69 percent when coordinated through DxO. However, on emergency department cases, DxO produced minimal accuracy or cost changes over standalone frontier models, as both configurations scored around 85 percent.

## Clinical Trials at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center

Microsoft AI leadership stressed that laboratory benchmarks cannot replace real-world clinical evaluation. Dr. Dominic King, vice president of Health at Microsoft AI, confirmed that Microsoft plans to begin testing the system with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, Massachusetts, within the next couple of months, as reported by [The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/1016690/suleyman-microsoft-diagnostic-orchestrator-science-medical-superintelligence).

Under the planned trial, hospital patients will receive customary care from clinical staff, including triage, time with a specialist, treatments, investigations, and decision on whether it’s safe to discharge. Concurrently, consenting patients will have their clinical information evaluated by DxO, allowing researchers to compare the system's recommendations directly against the care decisions made by attending medical teams. The work builds on other regional trials, including Google's study published in The Lancet evaluating its AMIE diagnostic system at Beth Israel urgent care centers.

[[FIG3]]

## Limitations, Accountability, and the Road Ahead

Despite the test results, researchers and independent observers identified notable caveats in the paper. The NEJM cases used for testing are typically solved in hospital settings by subspecialists or multidisciplinary boards rather than lone generalists. The authors acknowledged that comparing MAI-DxO against specialist teams would likely narrow the performance margin.

Financial claims also require clinical scrutiny: the reported savings reflect algorithmic test choices within static historical cases rather than dynamic clinical billing or patient management. Outside studies highlight additional structural challenges. Earlier in 2026, Harvard and Beth Israel researchers demonstrated strong triage diagnostic reasoning from OpenAI's o1-preview model, but experts cite unresolved questions surrounding legal liability when automated recommendations fail. Furthermore, a 2025 study cited by [Gizmodo](https://gizmodo.com/microsoft-says-its-new-ai-is-more-than-twice-as-good-at-diagnosing-diseases-as-doctors-2000829562) showed that physicians who relied on AI detection tools during colonoscopies experienced a decline in performance once the software assistance was removed.

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman maintains that clinicians will remain central to medical delivery, emphasizing that the tool is intended to reduce paperwork and diagnostic fatigue rather than replace clinicians. Looking ahead, Suleyman stated that Microsoft is collaborating with the Mayo Clinic to train a health foundation model scheduled for release in 2027, aiming to support continuous predictive forecasting directly from electronic medical records.

faq.q: What is the Microsoft AI Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO)?
faq.a: MAI-DxO is an artificial intelligence diagnostic framework developed by Microsoft that coordinates multiple AI agents powered by OpenAI's GPT-5 to simulate a clinical panel, systematically asking questions, ordering tests, and determining diagnoses.

faq.q: How accurate was MAI-DxO in the Science study?
faq.a: In complex New England Journal of Medicine cases, MAI-DxO scored 83.2% accuracy compared to 36.1% for generalist physicians with references and 22% without. On emergency department cases from Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, it achieved 80.3% accuracy compared to 46.8% for physicians.

faq.q: Where and when will clinical trials take place?
faq.a: Microsoft plans to initiate real-world evaluations within the next couple of months at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, comparing the system's parallel assessments with consenting emergency and urgent care patients against decisions by human clinicians.

faq.q: What are the primary limitations noted by researchers?
faq.a: The study was conducted on past, simulated patient records rather than live clinical environments. Additionally, the system was compared against individual generalist physicians rather than the multidisciplinary specialist panels that typically manage such complex cases.
